patterns.name: Shall versus may ambiguity
patterns.plain: Wording that leaves unclear whether an agency must act or merely may act lets the duty be read as optional, so the command depends on later interpretation.
patterns.fix: Use shall for required acts, reserve may for true discretion, and state the consequence of inaction.

patterns.name: Shall consider instead of ensure
patterns.plain: Requiring an agency only to consider a factor lets it record that it thought about the factor and then act as it already planned.
patterns.fix: Require the agency to achieve or ensure a stated outcome, or to explain in writing how the factor changed the decision.

patterns.name: Feasibility and practicability qualifiers
patterns.plain: Phrases like to the extent practicable make a requirement depend on cost or feasibility, so regulated parties can argue that compliance is not required in their case.
patterns.fix: Replace the qualifier with a fixed standard, or define feasibility objectively and put the burden of showing infeasibility on the regulated party.

patterns.name: Good faith compliance shield
headings: Safe Harbor for "Good Faith" Safety Efforts
patterns.plain: Protecting those who made a good faith or reasonable effort turns a duty to comply into a duty to try, which is hard to disprove.
patterns.fix: Define required practices objectively and limit any good faith defense to named, verifiable steps with the burden on the defendant.

patterns.name: Qualified shall that resists court orders
patterns.plain: A duty qualified by the agency's judgment or available resources reads as mandatory but leaves room for discretion that courts will not override.
cues: subject to the availability of appropriations
patterns.fix: State the duty without judgment or resource qualifiers, or give a deadline and a defined remedy if the agency does not act.

patterns.name: Technical infeasibility as exemption
patterns.plain: Saying developers cannot fully explain their models is used to soften transparency duties, so disclosure is required only where technically feasible.
patterns.fix: Require disclosure of inputs, tests and outputs that can be measured, and do not condition them on explaining internal model workings.

patterns.name: Open ended key terms
patterns.plain: Key terms left undefined, or defined loosely, let different groups read the law differently, which shifts the real meaning to later disputes.
patterns.fix: Define each operative term in the bill with examples, and state that the definition applies throughout.

patterns.name: Near-identical defined terms
patterns.plain: A term defined in one section appears in a slightly different form elsewhere, leaving doubt whether the definition applies.
patterns.fix: Use each defined term in exactly one form and add a clause that the definition governs every use in the Act.

patterns.name: Definition by exclusion list
patterns.plain: Defining a term by what it does not include leaves unclear boundaries and invites disputes over excluded categories.
patterns.fix: State affirmatively what is covered, and keep any exclusion list short, closed and justified.

patterns.name: Lists and interpretive canons
patterns.plain: Enumerated lists of covered items can be read as excluding everything unlisted, and a short list before a general term can narrow it.
patterns.fix: Add a rule that lists are illustrative, state intended breadth, and avoid short example lists before catch-all terms.

patterns.name: Choice of measurement unit
patterns.plain: The unit a law uses to count harm, such as net jobs or average screen time, can make the same facts look small or large.
patterns.fix: Specify the unit in the bill, prefer distributional measures, and require reporting in more than one unit.

patterns.name: Baseline selection
patterns.plain: Comparing present conditions to a chosen starting year can make a new harm look like a continuation of existing trends.
patterns.fix: Fix the baseline year in the text with a stated reason, and require sensitivity checks against alternative baselines.

patterns.name: Averaging over long periods
patterns.plain: Measuring impact as an average across a year or an election cycle hides concentrated harms that occur in short windows.
patterns.fix: Require measurement over the specific high-risk windows as well as the overall period.

patterns.name: Aggregated populations hide harm
patterns.plain: Measuring effects across the whole workforce or population can hide harms concentrated in particular places or groups.
patterns.fix: Require results broken out by region, income, age and other affected groups.

patterns.name: Threshold for what counts
patterns.plain: A high or hard to prove threshold for what counts as harm or interference can leave almost nothing covered.
patterns.fix: Set thresholds from observable measures such as reach or timing, and avoid proof of outcome effects.

patterns.name: Narrow AI system definition
patterns.plain: A definition limited to large or fully autonomous models leaves out recommendation tools, fine-tuned models and decision support that people rely on.
patterns.fix: Define by function and effect on people, not by size or autonomy, and cover decision support.

patterns.name: Narrow definition of harm
patterns.plain: Requiring individual, demonstrable, direct harm excludes diffuse or systemic harms that no single person can prove.
patterns.fix: Define harm to include probabilistic, cumulative and population-level effects.

patterns.name: De minimis thresholds
patterns.plain: A minimum size below which a deployment is ignored can exempt many small deployments that together have large effects.
patterns.fix: Aggregate related deployments toward the threshold and set it on cumulative effect.

patterns.name: Who runs impact assessments
patterns.plain: When the company or its chosen auditor controls the methodology and conduct of an assessment, the assessment may reflect the company's preferences.
patterns.fix: Require independent assessors chosen by the regulator, with methodology set in rules.

patterns.name: Counterfactual comparison
patterns.plain: Comparing impact against what would have happened anyway makes the added contribution of a technology look small.
patterns.fix: Measure absolute and incremental effects separately and do not net out assumed trends.

patterns.name: Easy metrics over important ones
headings: Measuring What's Measurable Versus What Matters
patterns.plain: Reporting duties built around easy numbers such as compute or API calls can leave out harder to measure harms such as loss of autonomy.
patterns.fix: Require measures tied to outcomes for people, with qualitative evidence where numbers are weak.

patterns.name: Proof of causation required first
patterns.plain: Requiring established causal proof before action can delay rules until effects are entrenched, since long term harms take years to document.
patterns.fix: Allow action on credible evidence of risk and use a reasonable likelihood standard.

patterns.name: Foreseeability requirement
patterns.plain: Limiting liability to foreseeable harm leaves out unexpected behavior of complex systems, which is a main concern.
patterns.fix: Pair foreseeability with duties to test for unknown risks, or apply strict liability for high-risk uses.

patterns.name: Individual proof for systemic harm
patterns.plain: Frameworks that require one person to prove one system caused one injury cannot address effects visible only across populations.
patterns.fix: Allow proof by population-level evidence and statistical showings.

patterns.name: Speculative benefits weighed against harm
patterns.plain: Cost-benefit rules that count uncertain future gains against documented present harms can tip decisions toward inaction.
patterns.fix: Require equal evidence standards on both sides and discount uncertain benefits.

patterns.name: Assumed job reabsorption
headings: "New Jobs Will Emerge" as Statutory Assumption
patterns.plain: Methods that assume displaced workers will find new roles leave out harm in cases where transitions are faster or harder than before.
patterns.fix: Measure realized outcomes for displaced workers and do not assume reabsorption.

patterns.name: Benchmark based compliance
patterns.plain: Compliance measured by fixed benchmarks can be met by tuning to the test while real-world performance differs.
patterns.fix: Require varied and updated tests including real-world outcome monitoring.

patterns.name: Preemption of state law
patterns.plain: Unclear or broad preemption language can replace stronger state laws with a weaker federal rule, or leave a patchwork that is later used to argue for a single weaker standard.
patterns.fix: State plainly whether the federal rule is a floor or a ceiling and list which state laws are preserved.

patterns.name: Split agency responsibility
patterns.plain: Authority divided or overlapping among agencies or committees leaves no single accountable body and gives regulated parties several venues.
patterns.fix: Name one lead agency with clear authority and a duty to resolve overlaps.

patterns.name: Exemption of federal entities
patterns.plain: Requirements that apply to others but exclude federal agencies leave the largest public users outside the rule.
patterns.fix: Apply the requirements to federal agencies or explain each exclusion and set an equal standard.

patterns.name: Choice of regulator
patterns.plain: Which agency oversees a subject shapes its culture and priorities, and some choices produce weaker or fragmented oversight.
cues: national institute of standards and technology
patterns.fix: Assign oversight to the agency with enforcement authority and expertise, with stated resources.

patterns.name: Policy and enforcement in different bodies
patterns.plain: Assigning rulemaking and enforcement to separate bodies with different standards lets each point to the other when gaps appear.
patterns.fix: Place both functions in one agency or require shared standards and a joint accountability mechanism.

patterns.name: Developer versus deployer duties
patterns.plain: When duties are divided between those who build and those who use a system without a clear rule, each can point to the other.
patterns.fix: Assign duties to each role and add joint and several liability where responsibility is shared.

patterns.name: Platform versus model liability
patterns.plain: If the law does not say whether model makers, platforms or users are responsible, no party is clearly liable for harmful output.
patterns.fix: Specify the liable party for each type of harm and how liability is shared.

patterns.name: Extraterritorial reach unclear
patterns.plain: Silence or vague wording on whether the law reaches foreign conduct invites arguments that it does not, and foreign firms may escape duties domestic ones bear.
patterns.fix: State the reach of the law, the jurisdictional hooks, and the agent for service of process for foreign firms.

patterns.name: Jurisdiction shopping provisions
patterns.plain: Jurisdictional hooks that depend on where a company locates operations let it choose the place with the lightest rules.
patterns.fix: Tie coverage to where people are affected, not where the company operates.

patterns.name: Mutual recognition of foreign rules
headings: Mutual Recognition Agreements as Downward Pressure
patterns.plain: Treating weaker foreign regulation as equivalent can lower the effective standard for companies that comply abroad.
patterns.fix: Define equivalence by objective criteria and give the regulator authority to revoke findings.

patterns.name: Military tools reused domestically
patterns.plain: Systems built for military use may be reused for domestic policing and fall outside rules written for civilian products.
patterns.fix: Apply the rules to any use in domestic law enforcement regardless of the system's origin.

patterns.name: No cooling-off period
patterns.plain: Without a waiting period for officials moving to regulated firms, the agency can become a training ground for industry staff.
patterns.fix: Add post-service restrictions and conflict of interest rules for agency staff and board members.

patterns.name: Delayed effective dates
patterns.plain: A law may take effect years after passage with extensions built in, leaving time for conditions to change or for it to be amended or defunded.
patterns.fix: Use a short fixed effective date, and limit any extension to one with stated conditions and reporting.

patterns.name: Sunset clauses
patterns.plain: A provision that expires unless renewed lets opponents end it by blocking reauthorization instead of repealing it.
patterns.fix: Avoid sunsets for core duties, or make renewal automatic unless Congress acts to end it.

patterns.name: Deadlines without consequences
patterns.plain: A deadline for agency action with no consequence for missing it is often ignored, since courts are reluctant to enforce timelines.
patterns.fix: Add a default rule, such as an interim rule taking effect, or a right to sue if the deadline passes.

patterns.name: Activation depends on a finding
patterns.plain: A mandate that begins only after an official finding or determination may never operate if no one makes the finding.
patterns.fix: Set a default effective date and require a published decision by a deadline with reasons.

patterns.name: Grandfathering and prospective-only rules
patterns.plain: Applying rules only to new conduct or new systems exempts existing actors and systems, so impact is felt gradually if at all.
cues: in effect on the date of enactment
prior to the date of enactment
patterns.fix: Apply rules to existing actors on a defined schedule and set an end date for any exemption.

patterns.name: Silence on retroactivity
patterns.plain: A law silent on retroactivity is presumed not to reach past conduct, which can leave existing violations untouched.
patterns.fix: State whether the rule applies to conduct before enactment and how continuing violations are treated.

patterns.name: Pilot programs without a path
headings: Pilot-to-Mandate Gateways With No Forcing Function
patterns.plain: A pilot can be extended or redesigned without ever scaling, and the outcome can be read either as proof that it is enough or that it does not work.
patterns.fix: Set a fixed end date and a rule that the program expands automatically unless Congress or the agency decides otherwise.

patterns.name: Pre versus post deployment standards
patterns.plain: Favoring monitoring after release over testing before release leaves harms to be corrected after the fact, which does not help when effects cannot be reversed.
patterns.fix: Require testing before release for high-risk uses along with ongoing monitoring.

patterns.name: Too early to regulate arguments
patterns.plain: Readiness reviews or short reauthorization windows can make the right time to regulate always later, since technology keeps changing.
patterns.fix: Use performance-based duties that adapt to change, rather than waiting for stability.

patterns.name: Waiting period for market solutions
patterns.plain: Requiring market-based or voluntary solutions to be tried first builds in a waiting period while harm continues, and insufficient is rarely defined.
patterns.fix: Define when voluntary measures are insufficient and set a deadline after which mandates apply.

patterns.name: Consultation with international partners
patterns.plain: A duty to consult or align with international partners can delay action until consensus is reached, which may take years.
patterns.fix: Allow domestic action to proceed while consultation continues, with a fixed time limit.

patterns.name: No duty after release
headings: No Ongoing Maintenance or Update Obligations
patterns.plain: Without ongoing duties, companies can release systems and leave them in use without updates or support while they keep making consequential decisions.
patterns.fix: Require maintenance, security updates and a notice before withdrawing support for systems in use.

patterns.name: Updates do not retrigger review
patterns.plain: If minor updates do not require new review, a system can change substantially over time without fresh evaluation.
patterns.fix: Define substantial modification by measurable change and require re-evaluation when it occurs.

patterns.name: Order of obligations
patterns.plain: Putting disclosure duties first and safety standards later gives time to influence the later rules while the consequences come last.
patterns.fix: Phase obligations so safety duties take effect no later than disclosure duties.

patterns.name: Chained prerequisites
patterns.plain: Provisions that each require an earlier step can be reasonable alone but together make implementation depend on a long chain.
patterns.fix: Limit dependencies, give each step a deadline, and provide a default if a step is missed.

patterns.name: Transition timelines slower than change
headings: Transition Timelines Disconnected From Actual Displacement Speed
patterns.plain: Multi-year timelines for support or compliance can lag changes that happen within months, leaving affected people without help.
patterns.fix: Tie timelines to measured speed of change and include triggers to accelerate.

patterns.name: Emergency authorizations without end
patterns.plain: Emergency approvals with no end date or compliance requirement allow systems to become entrenched.
patterns.fix: Add a sunset, reporting and a later compliance date to any emergency authorization.

patterns.name: Takes effect when others act
patterns.plain: Provisions that apply only when other countries adopt matching measures may remain inactive indefinitely.
patterns.fix: Set an independent effective date with a review rather than waiting on foreign action.

patterns.name: Waiver and exemption authority
patterns.plain: Authority to grant waivers for good cause or hardship, especially without notice to Congress or the public, can be used selectively to reduce the law's effect.
patterns.fix: Limit waivers by criteria, time, and public notice, with reporting to Congress.

patterns.name: Broad safe harbors
headings: Safe Harbors That Swallow the Rule
patterns.plain: A safe harbor deeming certain conduct compliant can be broad enough to cover most of the behavior the prohibition was meant to address.
patterns.fix: Narrow the safe harbor to defined practices, make presumptions rebuttable and review them periodically.

patterns.name: Notwithstanding clauses
patterns.plain: Notwithstanding language overrides other law, and its scope, whether the Act or the code and whether it covers regulations, is often unclear.
cues: notwithstanding any other provision of law
notwithstanding any other provision of this act
patterns.fix: List the specific provisions overridden and state whether regulations are included.

patterns.name: Or as otherwise provided by law
headings: Strategic Use of "Or as Otherwise Provided by Law"
patterns.plain: Language excepting what is otherwise provided by law can let later statutes or regulations create exceptions the drafters never reviewed.
cues: or as otherwise provided by law
except as otherwise provided by law
patterns.fix: Cite the specific laws that create exceptions, and limit to those in effect at enactment.

patterns.name: Provisions readable two ways
patterns.plain: A sentence prohibiting conduct except in compliance with a standard can read as both a ban and a permission, depending on where the standard is set.
patterns.fix: Separate the prohibition from the permitted conduct and define permissions by named conditions.

patterns.name: National security carve-out
patterns.plain: Broad exemptions or waivers for national security can be defined widely enough to cover surveillance, policing and border uses.
patterns.fix: Define the exemption narrowly, require specific findings, and add oversight reporting.

patterns.name: Trade secret exemptions
headings: Trade Secret Exemptions for Algorithmic Transparency
patterns.plain: Trade secret protection can limit disclosure to high-level descriptions, withholding detail needed for independent evaluation.
patterns.fix: Allow confidential disclosure to regulators and vetted auditors and bar use of trade secret claims to block review.

patterns.name: Open source exemption
patterns.plain: How open source is defined decides whether an exemption covers genuinely open projects or large companies releasing parts of their models.
patterns.fix: Define open source by license terms and exclude commercial deployments at scale.

patterns.name: Consent by clicking agree
patterns.plain: Treating a click on lengthy terms as consent satisfies the law's wording while giving users little real choice.
patterns.fix: Require clear, specific, separate consent and bar consent as a substitute for core duties.

patterns.name: Parental controls as safe harbor
patterns.plain: Offering parental controls can be treated as meeting the duty, shifting responsibility to parents who may lack technical knowledge.
patterns.fix: Keep duties on the company and treat parental tools as an addition and not a defense.

patterns.name: Synthetic data exemption
headings: Synthetic Data as a Regulatory Escape
patterns.plain: Data generated from personal data may be treated as outside privacy rules, even though it carries information derived from individuals.
patterns.fix: Treat data derived from personal data as covered unless re-identification is shown to be impossible.

patterns.name: Classification as escape
patterns.plain: Systems designated classified fall outside public review, and records requests and challenges become effectively impossible.
patterns.fix: Provide cleared oversight bodies with access and require periodic declassification review.

patterns.name: Manipulation versus persuasion
patterns.plain: Requiring deceptive intent or coercion before something counts as manipulation leaves out engagement design that exploits users without such intent.
patterns.fix: Define manipulation by effect on users and by design features, without requiring proof of intent.

patterns.name: Content neutral framing
patterns.plain: Treating algorithmic curation as content neutral leaves amplification of harmful material outside rules aimed at content.
patterns.fix: Regulate design and amplification features directly, regardless of content.

patterns.name: Narrow synthetic content definition
patterns.plain: Requiring content to be entirely AI-generated leaves out mixed content that a person edited from an AI draft.
patterns.fix: Cover content that is wholly or substantially generated or altered by AI.

patterns.name: Narrow deepfake definition
headings: Defining "Deepfake" to Exclude Most Synthetic Media
patterns.plain: A narrow deepfake definition can exclude fake news text, synthetic images of invented events and made-up quotes.
patterns.fix: Define by deception of a reasonable viewer and include text, image, audio and video.

patterns.name: Narrow addictive design definition
patterns.plain: Tying addictive design to clinical criteria leaves out compulsive-use features, so engaging designs remain allowed while addictive ones are banned.
patterns.fix: Define by design features such as infinite scroll and variable rewards, with no clinical test.

patterns.name: Companion systems outside categories
patterns.plain: AI companions may not fit existing categories, so it can be argued that existing law is enough or does not apply.
patterns.fix: Add a category for emotionally interactive systems with specific duties.

patterns.name: Narrow vulnerable population definition
patterns.plain: A narrow list of vulnerable groups can leave out minors, people with cognitive decline, people in crisis and the economically desperate.
patterns.fix: Define vulnerability by circumstances and include a regulator power to expand it.

patterns.name: Incident reporting definitions
patterns.plain: Incident definitions requiring physical harm or materiality exclude near-misses, statistical discrimination and gradual harms.
patterns.fix: Define incidents to include near-misses and non-physical harms, with low thresholds for reporting.

patterns.name: Risk tiers set narrowly
patterns.plain: Risk categories focused on physical safety leave out risks such as labor disruption, democratic erosion and concentration of power.
patterns.fix: Define risk to include societal, economic and civil rights harms.

patterns.name: Algorithmic versus AI label
patterns.plain: Choosing the term algorithmic or AI changes how broad a law appears, and the label can narrow or widen what is covered.
patterns.fix: Define the term by functions covered and use it consistently.

patterns.name: Displacement versus augmentation
patterns.plain: Regulating only replacement of workers leaves out augmentation that often turns into replacement over time.
patterns.fix: Cover tasks changed or reduced as well as full job loss.

patterns.name: Algorithmically managed workers
patterns.plain: Workers managed by algorithms may not be legally recognized as employees, leaving employment protections outside reach.
patterns.fix: Define employment by control and dependence, including algorithmic control.

patterns.name: Narrow export control definitions
patterns.plain: Narrow definitions of controlled technology cover specific models while training methods and know-how move freely.
patterns.fix: Define controlled items by capability and include methods and know-how.

patterns.name: Ambiguity that invites litigation
patterns.plain: Ambiguous terms and unclear standing invite legal challenges that can delay implementation for years.
patterns.fix: Define terms and standing clearly and add severability and expedited review.

patterns.name: Weak or absent enforcement
patterns.plain: A mandate with no private right of action, no penalties or only small fines gives little reason to comply, especially if the sole enforcer is underfunded.
patterns.fix: Add meaningful penalties, enforcement funding and a private right of action.

patterns.name: Judicial review limits
patterns.plain: Limits on which courts may hear challenges, short filing periods or deferential review standards can restrict or delay legal review.
patterns.fix: Set clear venue, reasonable filing times and the standard of review.

patterns.name: Exhaustion of remedies
patterns.plain: Requiring every administrative step before court can take years, by which time the issue may be moot.
patterns.fix: Set time limits for each step and allow court access if deadlines pass.

patterns.name: Unclear standing to sue
patterns.plain: When it is unclear who may sue, or affected communities have no way to challenge a deployment, enforcement depends on the agency's willingness.
patterns.fix: State who may sue and allow community and organization standing.

patterns.name: Unclear private right of action
headings: Strategic Ambiguity About Private Right of Action
patterns.plain: When courts split on whether a statute implies a private right of action, individuals may be able to sue in some places and not others.
patterns.fix: State expressly whether individuals may sue and for what remedies.

patterns.name: Burden placed on the enforcer
patterns.plain: Requiring regulators to prove harm without requiring companies to show safety makes enforcement slow and costly.
patterns.fix: Require developers to show safety for high-risk uses and shift the burden after a threshold showing.

patterns.name: Money only remedies
patterns.plain: Remedies limited to fines treat violations as a cost of business, while the ability to halt a system is a stronger deterrent.
patterns.fix: Include injunctive relief and the power to suspend a system.

patterns.name: Caps on damages and liability
patterns.plain: Statutory caps limit what injured people can recover, so losses above the cap fall on them instead of the company.
patterns.fix: Remove caps or index them to revenue and harm.

patterns.name: No structural remedies
patterns.plain: Excluding court power to order changes to algorithms or divestiture of data limits remedies to money.
patterns.fix: Authorize courts to order modifications, deletion of models and data divestiture.

patterns.name: Flat penalties that shrink with scale
headings: Penalty Structures That Diminish With Scale
patterns.plain: Flat per-violation penalties are small for large companies, while revenue-based penalties scale with size.
patterns.fix: Set penalties as the greater of a fixed sum or a percentage of revenue.

patterns.name: No notice of AI decisions
headings: Who Gets to Challenge AI Decisions
patterns.plain: Without notice that AI shaped a decision, affected people cannot know they have something to challenge.
patterns.fix: Require notice, explanation and an appeal path for AI-mediated decisions.

patterns.name: Arbitration and class waivers
headings: Mandatory Arbitration and Class Action Waivers
patterns.plain: Mandatory arbitration, class action waivers and individualized proof requirements prevent claims from being combined, leaving little remedy for widely shared harms.
patterns.fix: Bar pre-dispute arbitration and class waivers and allow aggregate proof.

patterns.name: Short limitations period
headings: Statute of Limitations for AI Harm
patterns.plain: A short filing period can close the window before many harms are discovered.
cues: after the date of the violation
patterns.fix: Start the clock at discovery and allow a longer period.

patterns.name: No board level duties
patterns.plain: Without duties at board level, responsibility rests with the company, which changes behavior less than personal accountability.
patterns.fix: Add oversight duties and personal liability for directors and officers in cases of knowing violation.

patterns.name: Defunding instead of repeal
patterns.plain: A spending rider barring enforcement leaves the law on the books but inactive, avoiding a visible repeal vote.
patterns.fix: Provide a dedicated funding source and a standing authority not dependent on annual riders.

patterns.name: Conditional appropriations
patterns.plain: Funding made conditional on certifications or reports means money does not flow if the condition is never met.
patterns.fix: Fund the work without conditions or give a default release of funds.

patterns.name: Cost scoring windows
patterns.plain: Provisions can be built so costs fall outside the budget scoring window, making the law appear free while costs arrive later.
patterns.fix: Report costs beyond the scoring period and avoid timing that moves costs out of it.

patterns.name: Mandates without money
patterns.plain: Requirements placed on state or local governments with no funding leave them to pay or not comply.
patterns.fix: Appropriate funds or condition the mandate on funding.

patterns.name: Authorized but not funded
patterns.plain: A large authorization number can make a program look funded while actual appropriations are far smaller.
cues: there are authorized to be appropriated
such sums as may be necessary
patterns.fix: Pair authorizations with mandatory funding or require reporting of the gap.

patterns.name: Underfunded duties force triage
patterns.plain: A mandate funded below the cost of full compliance leaves staff to choose which parts to enforce, since spending beyond appropriations risks personal liability.
cues: subject to the availability of appropriations
to the extent funds are available
patterns.fix: Match funding to duties or specify which duties take priority.

patterns.name: Regulator funded by industry fees
patterns.plain: A regulator funded by fees from those it regulates may face budget pressure when it enforces strongly.
patterns.fix: Fund the regulator through appropriations or insulate fee revenue from enforcement outcomes.

patterns.name: Tax treatment of AI investment
patterns.plain: Tax rules such as accelerated depreciation and credits make deployment profitable regardless of social effects.
patterns.fix: Review tax incentives alongside regulation and condition them on compliance.

patterns.name: No insurance requirement
patterns.plain: Without mandatory liability insurance, there is no outside assessment of risk and no guaranteed funds for injured people.
patterns.fix: Require insurance or bonding scaled to risk.

patterns.name: Gains go to capital
patterns.plain: With no mechanism for sharing productivity gains, benefits accrue to owners, and transition funds can be described as penalizing innovation.
patterns.fix: Include a defined mechanism for sharing gains or funding transitions.

patterns.name: Undefined standards left to agencies
patterns.plain: Terms like reasonable or appropriate left undefined push hard choices to agencies, whose rules can then be challenged and delayed.
patterns.fix: Define standards in the bill or give objective criteria and a deadline for the rule.

patterns.name: Layered rulemaking requirements
patterns.plain: Stacked analyses and consultations before a rule takes effect add months or years, and each creates a record open to challenge.
patterns.fix: Limit analytic steps, set a total deadline and allow interim rules.

patterns.name: Cross-references and incorporation
patterns.plain: Defining terms by reference to other laws or private documents makes the law hard to read and shifts meaning if the source changes.
patterns.fix: Restate key definitions in the text and fix the version of any referenced document.

patterns.name: Guidance functioning as law
patterns.plain: Guidance documents and letters are not binding but are treated as law by regulated parties, can change without notice and comment and operate out of public view.
patterns.fix: Require notice and comment for guidance with significant effect and publish it centrally.

patterns.name: Private and industry standards
patterns.plain: Requiring compliance with industry or private standards hands rule content to standards bodies where regulated parties are heavily represented.
patterns.fix: Specify required outcomes in the bill, adopt standards by rule and require balanced participation in standards bodies.

patterns.name: Delegation through several layers
patterns.plain: Authority passed from agency to sub-agency to regional or local bodies compounds discretion until the original mandate is hard to recognize.
patterns.fix: Limit delegation depth and require reporting on how each level applies the mandate.

patterns.name: Certification gatekeepers
patterns.plain: Compliance through certified processes or accredited bodies can stall if the infrastructure does not exist, or can depend on certifiers paid by those they certify.
patterns.fix: Set up certification capacity before the duty applies, limit certifier conflicts and allow alternatives.

patterns.name: Incorporation as amended
patterns.plain: Referencing standards as amended from time to time changes the law's content without a new vote, handing control to whoever maintains the document.
cues: as amended from time to time
patterns.fix: Fix the referenced version by date and require review before adopting changes.

patterns.name: Stacked advisory bodies
patterns.plain: Seats set aside for industry or members chosen for industry experience can give regulated parties the leading role in drafting the rules.
patterns.fix: Set balanced membership with public interest seats, conflict rules and published recommendations.

patterns.name: Record and comment flooding
patterns.plain: Record requirements and duties to respond to comments reward large volumes of submissions, which can be used to build a litigation record or overwhelm review.
patterns.fix: Allow the agency to group duplicate comments and limit response duty to distinct issues.

patterns.name: Stakeholder process design
patterns.plain: Consensus requirements in stakeholder processes give a veto to industry, and expertise weighting or short timelines can marginalize civil society.
patterns.fix: Replace consensus with majority rules, fund participation and set adequate timelines.

patterns.name: Comment period timing
patterns.plain: Short comment windows for complex rules, including over holidays, limit public participation.
patterns.fix: Set comment periods in proportion to complexity, with minimum lengths.

patterns.name: Limits on regulator capacity
patterns.plain: Barring internal testing tools, requiring third-party assessments or low pay scales reduces the regulator's own ability to evaluate.
patterns.fix: Fund in-house testing capacity and competitive pay for technical roles.

patterns.name: Reports and studies instead of action
headings: Reporting Requirements as Substitutes for Action
patterns.plain: Requiring a study or report in place of a concrete outcome gives the appearance of progress while action is deferred.
patterns.fix: Attach an action or default rule to each report and set deadlines.

patterns.name: Sequential studies
patterns.plain: Chained assessments each with its own timeline, comment period and challenge mean implementation is always one study away.
patterns.fix: Limit to one study with a deadline and an automatic next step.

patterns.name: Transparency defined thinly
patterns.plain: A bare statement that content is AI-generated is less informative than disclosing training data and limitations, and laws can require only the former.
patterns.fix: List the required disclosures such as data sources, limits and test results.

patterns.name: Labeling as the whole solution
patterns.plain: Labeling is inexpensive and may have little effect on belief, but can be treated as sufficient in place of structural measures.
patterns.fix: Treat labels as one measure and keep structural duties.

patterns.name: Control of evidence
patterns.plain: Companies hold the data needed to prove harm, and without disclosure powers, subpoena authority or preservation duties, regulators and plaintiffs cannot get it.
patterns.fix: Add disclosure, subpoena and preservation powers.

patterns.name: Log retention missing
headings: Destroying the Evidentiary Trail by Design
patterns.plain: Without record retention duties, systems can minimize logging, which makes later accountability difficult.
patterns.fix: Require retention of logs and decision records for a fixed period.

patterns.name: Researcher and journalist access
patterns.plain: Without statutory access rights, independent evaluation depends on company goodwill that can be withdrawn.
patterns.fix: Provide legal access for vetted researchers and safe harbor for good faith research.

patterns.name: Missing whistleblower protection
patterns.plain: Employees are a likely source of safety information, and without protection they can be silenced or penalized.
patterns.fix: Add anti-retaliation protection, confidential channels and remedies.

patterns.name: NDAs limit safety disclosure
patterns.plain: If nondisclosure agreements stay fully enforceable, or exceptions apply only to confidential regulatory channels, employees may be unable to report safety concerns.
patterns.fix: Declare NDAs unenforceable for disclosures of safety or legal violations to any lawful recipient.

patterns.name: Audit frequency and scope
patterns.plain: Annual or narrowly scoped audits miss fast-changing systems and misuse.
patterns.fix: Require audits at major changes with scope covering misuse.

patterns.name: Training data records
headings: Training Data Provenance Requirements (or Lack Thereof)
patterns.plain: Without provenance requirements, data of uncertain origin cannot be traced and inputs stay unaccountable.
patterns.fix: Require documentation of training data sources and rights.

patterns.name: Retention versus deletion tension
patterns.plain: The tension between keeping records for accountability and deleting data for privacy can be invoked either way depending on convenience.
patterns.fix: Reconcile in the text with a retention schedule for accountability records and a privacy-protective access regime.

patterns.name: Reported but not published
headings: What Must Be Reported Versus What Must Be Published
patterns.plain: Reports sent to regulators without public release prevent public pressure and comparison.
patterns.fix: Require public release of reports with narrow redactions.

patterns.name: Reports that cannot be compared
patterns.plain: Reporting formats that differ between companies produce data that cannot be meaningfully compared.
patterns.fix: Require a standard reporting template and metrics.

patterns.name: Reporting too infrequent
patterns.plain: Annual reporting for systems that change weekly means information is always outdated.
patterns.fix: Set reporting frequency to match change speed and require event-driven reports.

patterns.name: Severability used strategically
patterns.plain: A severability clause can keep less visible provisions alive when others fall, while omitting one can make challenges to the whole law riskier or safer.
cues: if any provision of this act
patterns.fix: Include a clear severability clause and consider which provisions are essential.

patterns.name: Savings clause without substance
patterns.plain: A clause preserving existing rights can be empty if the new framework makes those rights hard to use in practice.
cues: nothing in this act shall be construed
shall not be construed to diminish
patterns.fix: Back the savings clause with operative rules that keep the rights usable.

patterns.name: Preemption of tort and common law
headings: Strategic Silence on Preemption of Common Law Claims
patterns.plain: Silence on state common law claims, or a freeze on legal frameworks, leaves doubt over whether courts may develop liability theories.
patterns.fix: State whether state tort and common law claims are preserved.

patterns.name: Repeal by conflicting later law
headings: Constructive Repeal Through Irreconcilable Later Enactment
patterns.plain: A later statute that is hard to reconcile with an earlier one leaves both on the books, creating uncertainty settled only by litigation.
patterns.fix: Repeal or amend the earlier provisions expressly.

patterns.name: Placement within the code
headings: Strategic Placement Within the U.S. Code
patterns.plain: Where a provision is codified affects which agency runs it, which committees oversee it and which precedents apply.
patterns.fix: Choose placement with the intended regime and agency in mind and state it.

patterns.name: Section 230 interactions
patterns.plain: Whether algorithmic curation counts as publishing or neutral hosting is unresolved, and the bill may be silent on it.
patterns.fix: State how Section 230 applies to AI-generated and algorithmically curated content.

patterns.name: Output as original work
patterns.plain: Treating AI outputs as original works can reduce the leverage of rights holders over the use of their work for training.
patterns.fix: Address training use and output ownership expressly in the text.

patterns.name: Preemption of anti-discrimination law
patterns.plain: Weaker AI-specific standards may displace stronger claims under existing civil rights laws.
patterns.fix: Add a clause preserving existing civil rights and consumer protections.

patterns.name: Intellectual property interplay
patterns.plain: Patents, copyrightable outputs and trade secret model weights together can limit auditing and competition.
patterns.fix: Allow audit access notwithstanding IP claims and address output ownership.

patterns.name: Contract terms override public law
patterns.plain: Without anti-waiver provisions, contracts of adhesion can set aside protections the statute gives.
patterns.fix: Make protections non-waivable by contract.

patterns.name: Authority open to major questions challenge
patterns.plain: Grants of authority just ambiguous enough to be challenged under the major questions doctrine can face years of litigation.
patterns.fix: State the authority and its limits clearly, with specific findings on scope.

patterns.name: Ambiguity after Chevron
patterns.plain: With deference to agency readings gone, vague language is resolved by courts, which can delay or reverse agency interpretation.
patterns.fix: Draft specifically or give express discretion to the agency.

patterns.name: Findings sections and constitutionality
headings: Strategic Use of "Findings" Sections to Manufacture Deference
patterns.plain: Congressional findings shape how courts judge a law's constitutionality, and well-drafted or weakened findings change its vulnerability.
patterns.fix: Include specific findings supported by record evidence.

patterns.name: Legislative veto provisions
patterns.plain: Legislative veto provisions are unenforceable but agencies often comply, creating congressional control through political norms.
patterns.fix: Use joint resolutions subject to presentment instead of one-house vetoes.

patterns.name: Provisions exposed to First Amendment challenge
headings: Designing Provisions to Fail First Amendment Challenges
patterns.plain: Slightly overbroad provisions may be struck, and the resulting decision can narrow regulatory space for a generation.
patterns.fix: Narrowly tailor speech-related provisions and document the interest served.

patterns.name: Takings exposure
patterns.plain: Data sharing or forced access provisions can draw takings challenges that could limit regulation of whole categories.
patterns.fix: Provide compensation or voluntary licensing where taking risks arise.

patterns.name: Due process vulnerability
patterns.plain: Aggressive procedures with vague standards invite due process challenges that can remove enforcement while leaving the law in place.
patterns.fix: Pair enforcement powers with clear standards and procedural protections.

patterns.name: Dormant commerce clause challenges
patterns.plain: Vulnerable state laws can generate litigation that supports arguments for a weaker federal standard.
patterns.fix: Draft federal law to preserve state authority and avoid reliance on vulnerable state measures.

patterns.name: Sense of Congress language
headings: Sense of Congress Resolutions Masquerading as Action
patterns.plain: A sense of Congress statement has no legal force but can be presented as if Congress took a position.
patterns.fix: Replace with an operative provision or remove it.

patterns.name: Preamble goals without operative force
patterns.plain: A preamble declares bold goals while operative provisions contain qualifications that keep the goals from being achieved.
cues: it is the policy of the united states
patterns.fix: Align operative text with each stated goal and state that purposes guide interpretation.

patterns.name: Innovation and competitiveness findings
patterns.plain: Findings that regulation could cause the country to fall behind competitors can shape later rulemaking and cost-benefit analysis.
patterns.fix: Keep competitiveness language out of mandatory analytical tests.

patterns.name: Voluntary commitments as substitute
patterns.plain: Voluntary pledges cited as proof that law is unnecessary can later be written into the law as its standard.
patterns.fix: Treat commitments as a floor and require enforceable duties.

patterns.name: Tool framing
patterns.plain: Describing AI as a tool can limit responsibility and block rules suited to autonomous systems.
patterns.fix: Assign duties by function and degree of autonomy.

patterns.name: Bias treated as a technical bug
headings: Embedding the "Bias Is a Bug" Frame
Embedding the "Bias Is a Bug, Not a Feature" Frame
patterns.plain: Framing bias as a technical defect makes the remedy to improve the system and not to limit its use.
patterns.fix: Allow use limits and outcome tests and not only technical fixes.

patterns.name: Human review requirement
patterns.plain: A human review requirement can create the appearance of oversight when reviewers tend to accept the system's output.
patterns.fix: Define meaningful review with authority, time and training and measure override rates.

patterns.name: Assistance that does not assist
patterns.plain: Retraining or support programs that are underfunded, mismatched or hard to qualify for give the appearance of addressing displacement.
patterns.fix: Fund and target assistance with measurable eligibility and outcomes.

patterns.name: Impact assessments without effect
patterns.plain: Informational assessments that do not affect deployment decisions show communities their harm while deployment goes ahead.
patterns.fix: Link assessment findings to approval, mitigation duties or a right to object.

patterns.name: Adversary will do it anyway argument
headings: The "Adversary Will Do It Anyway" Argument
patterns.plain: Framing every safety rule as helping a rival nation presents restraint as surrender and can crowd out safety measures.
patterns.fix: Require stated evidence on competitive claims and keep safety duties independent.

patterns.name: Compliance costs that favor incumbents
patterns.plain: Heavy compliance requirements can act as barriers that large firms can absorb and smaller or open source competitors cannot.
patterns.fix: Scale obligations to size and risk and offer support to small entrants.

patterns.name: Data moat through privacy rules
headings: Data Moat Protection Through Privacy Framing
patterns.plain: Privacy rules limiting new collection can leave established firms with historic data while new entrants have none.
patterns.fix: Assess competitive effects of privacy rules and allow data access for competitors.

patterns.name: Compute thresholds
patterns.plain: Thresholds set to capture only the largest labs impose costs that only well-resourced firms can handle and leave others unregulated.
patterns.fix: Use capability and risk measures, with thresholds updated by the regulator.

patterns.name: API level regulation
headings: API Access as a Regulatory Chokepoint
patterns.plain: Rules at the API level make API controllers gatekeepers and can end open source distribution.
patterns.fix: Regulate by use and risk and protect open distribution where risk is low.

patterns.name: Government procurement as standard
headings: Government Procurement as De Facto Standard-Setting
patterns.plain: Federal procurement rules effectively set industry standards with little public scrutiny and can favor incumbents.
patterns.fix: Publish procurement criteria for comment and review their market effects.

patterns.name: Weak portability standards
patterns.plain: Weak portability standards preserve switching costs while appearing pro-competitive.
patterns.fix: Require standard formats and real-time access with interoperability.

patterns.name: Interoperability mandates or absence
patterns.plain: Without interoperability, network effects lock in leading providers, so the choice is a market structure decision.
patterns.fix: Include interoperability duties for dominant services.

patterns.name: Vertical integration permissions
patterns.plain: Rules applying to one layer favor integrated firms that can shift costs between layers.
patterns.fix: Regulate across layers and restrict self-preferencing.

patterns.name: Acquisition review thresholds
patterns.plain: High thresholds or price-based tests, often zero for free AI products, exempt most acquisitions.
patterns.fix: Add review triggers based on data, users and capability.

patterns.name: Narrow ban implying permission
patterns.plain: Prohibiting one specific act can be read as allowing closely related conduct that the text does not mention.
patterns.fix: Add a general prohibition and state that unlisted related conduct is not authorized.

patterns.name: Permit with no decision deadline
patterns.plain: A permit or approval requirement with no deadline for the agency lets applications wait indefinitely, so approval may never arrive.
patterns.fix: Set a decision deadline with automatic approval or a right to sue if it is missed.

patterns.name: Conference committee rewrites
patterns.plain: Final text is reconciled by a small committee, so changes can occur with limited transparency after both chambers have debated.
patterns.fix: Require a waiting period and public posting of conference text before votes.

patterns.name: Signing statements
patterns.plain: Presidential statements on how ambiguous provisions will be read signal how the law will be enforced without a vote.
patterns.fix: Draft provisions specifically and track statements for effect.

patterns.name: Riders and omnibus bundling
patterns.plain: Unrelated provisions placed in must-pass bills receive little scrutiny and can change unrelated policy areas.
patterns.fix: Require germane amendments and posting time for large bills.

patterns.name: Retroactive redefinition
patterns.plain: A later law that clarifies an earlier one can reinterpret it in ways that conflict with original intent or settled court rulings.
cues: shall be deemed to have always
patterns.fix: Review later clarifying provisions against the original purpose and court readings.

patterns.name: Staged legislative history
patterns.plain: Floor statements and reports can be prepared to narrow or contradict plain text, and courts sometimes consult them.
patterns.fix: Write the intended meaning into the text itself.

patterns.name: Enrolled bill doctrine
headings: The Enrolled Bill Doctrine as Cover
patterns.plain: Once signed, the enrolled text is treated as conclusive even where it differs from what chambers voted on.
patterns.fix: Check enrolled text against passed text before signature.

patterns.name: Self-executing House rules
patterns.plain: A special rule can deem a bill passed without a separate vote, embedding policy that skips normal deliberation.
patterns.fix: Require separate recorded votes on substantive text.

patterns.name: Holman rule and targeted defunding
headings: The Holman Rule and Targeted Defunding
patterns.plain: Amendments to spending bills can cut named employees' pay to one dollar, neutralizing enforcement without touching the statute.
patterns.fix: Protect enforcement positions through statute and track appropriations amendments.

patterns.name: Technical corrections used for substance
patterns.plain: Bills presented as fixing typos can make substantive changes that receive little scrutiny.
patterns.fix: Limit technical corrections to enumerated typographic fixes with review.

patterns.name: Congressional Review Act timing
headings: Drafting to Exploit the Congressional Review Act Window
patterns.plain: Rules finalized late in an administration can be repealed by the next Congress, and drafting affects how quickly rules can be finished.
patterns.fix: Set deadlines that allow rules to be finalized outside the review window.

patterns.name: Committee jurisdiction shopping
patterns.plain: Committee assignment sets the lens through which a bill is written, so routing to one committee over another shapes the result.
patterns.fix: Track referral and use joint referral where several interests apply.

patterns.name: Starving the regulator
patterns.plain: Limiting a regulator's technical expertise through funding and staffing can make enforcement look ineffective.
patterns.fix: Fund technical staff and report on capacity.

patterns.name: Age verification burden
headings: Age Verification as a Poison Pill
patterns.plain: Requiring age verification that is infeasible or invasive can generate opposition that sinks the whole bill.
patterns.fix: Use feasible age assurance with privacy protections.

patterns.name: Volume of technical submissions
patterns.plain: Submitting thousands of pages of technical documentation can obscure information through volume.
patterns.fix: Require summaries, standard formats and page limits for key submissions.
